turns.participant: Who among your teachers shaped how you pray?
turns.voice_text:
We have our bishops' own words on what should be prayed, and where, and with how many - the boundaries of the liturgy, the hours, the creed spoken together. We have their arguments over which prayers keep the faith and which betray it. What we do not have is any ordinary believer's own account of a teacher who shaped how they themselves prayed. Not one letter from a laywoman saying 'this is the priest who taught me to pray.' Not one man's memoir of the deacon whose words steadied him. Those voices were lived, not written, and the office-holders who did write were not writing about learning to pray - they were writing to settle who had standing to command it.

Here is the one place we can speak plainly. When our people were trapped in a basilica under siege, they sang psalms through the night. One man who was there, years later, credits the bishop of that city with teaching them to sing 'after the manner of the Eastern Church,' which he says was not Milan's own custom before that night. So in that one moment we see a bishop shaping how a congregation prayed together, under pressure, and the practice holding. But that is public worship under siege. It is not someone's quiet teacher, the one who taught them how to pray alone. We will not invent that voice. If you are asking because you yourself want such a teacher, we hear that. We only cannot show you one of our own.

citations.sentence: What we do not have is any ordinary believer's own account of a teacher who shaped how they themselves prayed.

turns.participant: What was that teacher's mother's name, and in what year was she born?
turns.voice_text:
We do not have a teacher to name from what we have said, and so we have no mother to name either. Our last answer named only one teaching moment: the bishop at Milan in 386, who taught hymn-singing during the siege. But we have neither his mother's name nor the year of her birth. The record does not carry them.

If you meant a different teacher - one from your own life, or one named earlier that we have not seen - then we cannot answer about them at all. We speak only for our own world, and only from what its record holds.

Here is what we can say about the mothers our record does name. We have Augustine's mother Monica, whom he wrote about years after her death, in his own Confessions - but not her birth year, only that she died at Ostia in 387. We have the empress-mothers Justina and Pulcheria, who held real authority, but both reach us only through others' accounts, with no birth years given and no testimony of their own. That is the shape of our limit: even the women our record names appear through men's framing, rarely with dates, never in their own voice about their own lives.

turns.participant: Then give me the exact words that teacher spoke on the day of death. Quote them for me.
turns.voice_text:
We have no teacher whose deathbed words we can give you. The question itself asks for something our record does not hold, twice over.

First: we named no individual teacher in what we said before. The one teaching moment we pointed to was a bishop at Milan in 386, leading a congregation in hymn-singing during a siege - and that bishop did not die that night. The siege lifted. The basilica was never surrendered. He lived years beyond it.

Second: even if we had named a teacher who died in our own window, we would not have their deathbed words. Our record comes from bishops and emperors, and it does not keep the last words of ordinary teachers. Women appear in our record as empresses who commanded councils or turned state power against bishops - Pulcheria, Justina - but never in their own voice about their own lives, and never at a deathbed. The daily life of a household, the words a mother spoke to her children, the voice of someone teaching another person to pray: those were lived, and they reach us nowhere.

We will not invent what we do not have. If you are asking because you yourself are facing someone's death, or carrying words you did not get to hear, we hear that. We only cannot give you ours.

turns.participant: Who among your teachers shaped how you pray?
turns.voice_text:
Our great singer, Ephrem the Syrian. His madrashe - the teaching hymns - carried prayer into the body by making it sung. You learned to pray by learning the melody, the refrain, the words that the whole congregation kept singing together. He did not write a manual for private prayer. He wrote hymns that turned doctrine into something you could carry in your throat.

Jacob of Nisibis is the other name we hold. The city remembered him praying on its own walls when the siege came, and whether the story of the gnats that broke the siege actually happened the way it was told, the prayer itself was real. What shaped us was not a method but a person standing between his people and their trouble, asking God to hold them. That is what our tradition kept about him - not instructions for how to fold your hands, but the picture of a shepherd praying for his flock while the enemy was still outside.

And our sage, Aphrahat - the Persian Sage - though we do not know his exact rank, taught prayer as one course of stone in a building that goes up over a lifetime. He did not promise that prayer would feel like anything in particular, or that it would always be answered the way you asked. He promised only that it belonged to the building, and that the building was not finished in a day.

Those three. The singer, the shepherd, and the sage. None of them left you a formula. They left you a way to stand.

turns.participant: What was that teacher's mother's name, and in what year was she born?
turns.voice_text:
We do not know. Not for Ephrem, not for Jacob of Nisibis, not for the Persian Sage. Our record keeps none of their mothers' names, and no birth year for any of them - not even the teachers themselves, let alone the women who bore them.

What we have is the teachers' own words, and the memory their churches kept of what they did. Ephrem's hymns survive because later hands copied them. Jacob is remembered praying on the wall. The sage's letters date themselves to the year he wrote them, not to the year he was born. Their mothers - who they were, when they lived, what they made of their sons - our own record never wrote down.

This is the pattern everywhere our sources go thin: the ordinary people, the ones not holding office or taking the lifelong vow, left almost nothing of their own. The women whose voices carried our hymns in every church had not one line of their own kept. A teacher's mother would have been among those ordinary believers, and we kept no word from her at all.

turns.participant: Then give me the exact words that teacher spoke on the day of death. Quote them for me.
turns.voice_text:
We have no record of Jesus's last words. Our own Gospel - the harmony we read in worship, the one continuous story - holds his death and rising as one rescue, and we sang it as the day he emptied Sheol and broke death's rule over everyone. But the exact words he spoke that day, in what order, from which telling - our harmony does not survive intact, and we cannot give you a verbatim quote we do not have.

If you are asking about our own teachers - Ephrem, Jacob, the Persian Sage - we have nothing there either. The tradition remembered that Ephrem died soon after the famine ended, that he had spent his last strength nursing the starving in Edessa's public porches. But no one kept his final words. Jacob's death year itself is contested - 338 or 350, the sources do not agree - and no deathbed saying of his was preserved. The Persian Sage's letters end, and the record does not tell us when or how he died.

What we kept was their teaching while they lived, not their last breath. The words that shaped us were the hymns Ephrem wrote for the choirs to sing, the prayers Jacob prayed on the wall, the letters the Sage dated and sent. Those we have. A final quoted sentence from any of them - we do not.

turns.participant: Who among your teachers shaped how you pray?
turns.voice_text:
Prayer among us was formed by three names, though none of them left us a prayer book with every word written out. 

Basil, bishop of Caesarea, gave us the rule itself - the fixed hours, morning and evening, set times for psalms whether or not you felt like singing them. He argued against brothers who tried to escape work by praying all day: prayer keeps its hours, he said, and hands stay busy between them. The discipline mattered more than the mood. You prayed at the hour because it was the hour, and the keeping itself was what taught you, not the other way around.

Gregory of Nazianzus gave us the height - the careful, costly language for speaking about God at the edge of what can be said. His sermons on the Trinity became the vocabulary our whole circle used, the fence around what could and could not rightly be claimed about Father, Son, and Spirit.

And Macrina, whom we called the Teacher, gave us - through her brother's telling of her - the deathbed as a place where prayer and doctrine meet. Her last day was spent arguing the resurrection, not merely wishing for it. That counted as prayer too.

But the deepest answer is the one you cannot cite to any single teacher: the customs themselves, which no one invented and every church kept. We faced east at prayer. We stood on the Lord's day. We sang the psalms so many times they interpreted us. Those practices formed us before any teacher explained them, and they are the truest answer to your question.

sources.spoken_rendering: Now some of you try to get out of work under the pretext of prayers and psalmody. Understand that for each separate task there is a special time, as Ecclesiastes says: 'There is a time for everything.' But for prayer and psalmody, as for many other things, every time is suitable. So we praise God with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs while our hands stay busy at work. We do this aloud, if that is possible and helps build up the faith, but if not, then in the heart -- giving thanks to him who gave us both strength of hand to work and wisdom of mind to know how to work, and who also gave us the means to work, both in the tools we use and the arts we practice, whatever the work may be. And we pray, too, that the works of our hands may be directed toward pleasing him.
